boundaries.evidence: The Definition accepts any finite label poset (Lambda, rhd): for Lambda empty the basis C is empty, C spans the zero R-module, and axioms (i)-(ii) are vacuous.
The only objects allowed to vanish are the spans A^{rhd lambda}, which the Definition permits to be zero (maximal labels); no division or cancellation occurs.
Axiom (i) of the Definition fixes the algebra unit by i(1)=1, and an index set T(lambda) with a single element contributes the one basis element c^lambda_st.

Definition: coefficient independence of the first index is explicit in axiom (ii). Empty and singleton T(lambda) are permitted; an empty cell is the zero module and its bilinear form is uniquely zero.

boundaries.reason: There is no interval or limiting parameter here; the only order is the finite strict partial order rhd on Lambda, whose minimal and maximal labels are ordinary labels rather than interval endpoints.
Finiteness is a hypothesis of the Definition (C, Lambda and every T(lambda) are finite), so nothing is selected from an infinite family and no choice principle enters.
This is a Definition introducing the term cellular basis, not a biconditional theorem; clauses (i)-(ii) are imposed as axioms, so no forward implication is separately owed.
No converse is asserted anywhere in the Definition: it does not claim that data failing (i) or (ii) admit no alternative cellular presentation.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement covers the empty partition directly: with no parts every multiplicity z_j(lambda) and every difference lambda_i - lambda_{i+1} is 0, so it is both e-regular and e-restricted.
The inequalities of the Statement are strict, z_j(lambda) < e and lambda_i - lambda_{i+1} < e, and they hold at the value 0, which the e=infinity clause makes vacuous.

Definition: a one-part partition (n) has multiplicity 1<e for every e>=2; it is e-restricted exactly when n<e. Composite finite e uses the same inequalities, without identifying it with a prime characteristic.

The conjugate dictionary in the Statement, z_i(lambda') = lambda_i - lambda_{i+1}, makes e-restrictedness of lambda equivalent to e-regularity of lambda', the degenerate shapes (n) and (1^n) included.

boundaries.reason: The parameter e ranges over the discrete set {2,3,4,...} plus the single conventional value infinity, whose case the Statement disposes of; no continuous endpoint or limit arises.
The two conditions are pointwise inequalities on the parts of one fixed partition compared against e, so there is nothing to select and no choice principle occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Forward direction of the Statement's conjugate criterion: if lambda is e-restricted then lambda' is e-regular, because the dictionary z_i(lambda')=lambda_i-lambda_{i+1} turns the inequalities lambda_i-lambda_{i+1}<e into the e-regularity multiplicities of lambda'.

Reverse direction of the same criterion: if lambda' is e-regular then lambda is e-restricted, since z_i(lambda')<e for all i reads back as lambda_i-lambda_{i+1}<e for all i under the same conjugate dictionary of the Statement.

boundaries.reason: No family, union, product or indexed aggregate occurs: e(F,q) is the least m with [m]_q=0, a predicate on single integers.

For q!=1 the identity [e]_q=(q^e-1)/(q-1) with q-1 nonzero turns [e]_q=0 into q^e=1, the forward half of the Statement's finite-exactly-when-root-of-unity claim.

citations.quote:
A **ring** is a set $R$ carrying two binary operations ([[def-binary-operation]]),
addition $+$ and multiplication $\cdot$, and two distinguished elements $0$ and
$1$ of $R$, such that

- **(R1)** $(R, +, 0)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): addition is
  associative and commutative, $0 + x = x = x + 0$ for every $x \in R$, and every
  $x \in R$ has an additive inverse;
- **(R2)** $(R, \cdot, 1)$ is a monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]):
  multiplication is associative and $1 \cdot x = x = x \cdot 1$ for every
  $x \in R$;
- **(R3)** multiplication distributes over addition **on both sides**: for all
  $x, y, z \in R$,

$$x \cdot (y + z) \;=\; x \cdot y + x \cdot z, \qquad (y + z) \cdot x \;=\; y \cdot x + z \cdot x .$$

We write $xy$ for $x \cdot y$, call $0$ the **zero** and $1$ the **identity** (or
**unity**) of $R$, write $-x$ for the additive inverse of $x$, and abbreviate
$x - y := x + (-y)$.

**Why "the" zero, "the" identity and "the" additive inverse are legitimate.**
Each of $0$ and $1$ is a two-sided identity for its own operation, and a binary
operation has at most one two-sided identity ([[lem-identity-unique]],
[[def-identity-element]]), so each is determined by the operation and the
notation is single-valued. An additive inverse of $x$ is an inverse in the
monoid $(R,+,0)$ ([[def-invertible-element]]), and in a monoid an element has at
most one inverse ([[lem-inverse-unique]]); so $-x$ names one element, and a
single equation $y + x = 0$ already forces $y = -x$.

**Convention: a ring has an identity.** Axiom (R2) asks for a *monoid*, so the
existence of $1$ is part of the definition and is not an extra hypothesis to be
carried around. This is the convention used throughout this library. A structure
satisfying (R1), (R3) and the associativity half of (R2), but not required to
have a multiplicative identity, is called a **non-unital ring** (also *rng*); it
is not called a ring here, and where such a structure occurs it is named as a
non-unital ring in as many words. The distinction has content: the companion
page exhibits a subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ that is closed under addition, additive
inverses and multiplication and is not a subring, precisely because it misses
the identity.

Nothing above requires $1 \ne 0$. A ring in which $1 = 0$ has exactly one
element; the companion page records it as the **zero ring**. Definitions that
need $1 \ne 0$ — integral domain, division ring, field — say so explicitly.

derivations.claim: If $k=0$ or $\ell=0$ then $1=0$ in $A$, so $A$ has exactly one element by [F1], namely $0$; then no nonzero idempotent exists and the two families are empty, $k=\ell=0$, and the empty map is the required bijection. Assume henceforth that $k,\ell\ge1$.

For central idempotents $e,f\in A$ the products $ef$ and $e(1-f)$ are central idempotents with $ef+e(1-f)=e$ and $ef\cdot e(1-f)=0$: centrality gives $(ef)a=e(fa)=e(af)=(ea)f=(ae)f=a(ef)$ and $(1-f)a=a-af=a-fa=a(1-f)$ for all $a\in A$; idempotence gives $(ef)^2=efef=e^2f^2=ef$ and $(1-f)^2=1-2f+f^2=1-f$, hence $e(1-f)e(1-f)=e^2(1-f)^2=e(1-f)$; distributivity gives $ef+e(1-f)=e(f+1-f)=e$ and $ef\cdot e(1-f)=e^2f(1-f)=0$.

If $e$ is primitive and $f$ is a central idempotent, then $ef\in\{0,e\}$: by step 1.2, $e=ef+e(1-f)$ exhibits $e$ as a sum of the two orthogonal central idempotents $ef$ and $e(1-f)$, so primitivity forces $ef=0$ or $e(1-f)=0$; in the second case step 1.2 gives $ef=ef+0=ef+e(1-f)=e$.

Fix $j\in\{1,\dots,\ell\}$. Since $1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$, distributivity and centrality give $f_j=f_j\cdot1=\sum_i f_je_i=\sum_i e_if_j$, and step 2.1 gives $e_if_j\in\{0,e_i\}$ for every $i$; since $f_j\ne0$, the set $S_j:=\{i: e_if_j=e_i\}$ is nonempty and $f_j=\sum_{i\in S_j}e_i$.

For every $j$ the set $S_j$ is a singleton: its elements $e_i$ are pairwise orthogonal nonzero central idempotents summing to $f_j$ by step 3.1, so if $S_j$ contained distinct $i\ne i'$ then $f_j=e_i+\sum_{i''\in S_j,\ i''\ne i}e_{i''}$ would exhibit $f_j$ as a sum of the two orthogonal central idempotents $e_i$ and $f_j-e_i$, both nonzero since multiplying the second sum by the nonzero idempotent $e_{i'}$ retrieves $e_{i'}$, contradicting primitivity of $f_j$; hence $S_j=\{i(j)\}$ and $f_j=e_{i(j)}$.
The map $j\mapsto i(j)$ is injective: if $i(j)=i(j')=i$ with $j\ne j'$, then $e_i=e_i^2=f_jf_{j'}=0$ by idempotence, centrality and pairwise orthogonality of the $f$'s, contradicting $e_i\ne0$.

The map $j\mapsto i(j)$ is surjective: from $f_j=e_{i(j)}$ for all $j$ and both decompositions, $\sum_je_{i(j)}=1=\sum_ie_i$; multiplying this equality by the central idempotent $e_i$ and using pairwise orthogonality of the $e$'s gives $e_i$ on the left when $i$ lies in the image of $j\mapsto i(j)$ and $0$ otherwise, while the right side is $e_i\ne0$; hence every $i$ lies in the image.

Steps 5.1 and 5.2 make $j\mapsto i(j)$ a bijection $\{1,\dots,\ell\}\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ with $f_j=e_{i(j)}$ for all $j$ by step 4.1; its inverse $\sigma$ satisfies $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$, and $k=\ell$. Since the families were arbitrary, the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is unique up to order, as claimed.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 disposes of k=0 or l=0: then 1=0 and A is the zero ring, both families are empty, and the empty map is the required bijection.
The zero ring 1=0 is handled in step 1.1 and the Statement omits zero parts from the families; the argument divides by nothing, so no other vanishing configuration needs exclusion.
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 treat a single primitive idempotent f_j and force its summand set S_j to be a singleton; the case k=l=1 with e_1=f_1 is the instance i(j)=1.
Step 2.1 forces ef in {0,e} for primitivity and step 4.1 collapses each S_j to one index, so an idempotent is never exhibited as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal central pieces.

boundaries.reason: The index sets are the finite sets {1,...,k} and {1,...,l}; no interval, extremal value or limiting boundary occurs in the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement records that no choice principle is used, the families being finite; step 3.1 forms S_j inside the finite index set {1,...,k}.

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts uniqueness of the two decompositions up to order, an equality of lengths and a matching bijection, not one direction of an equivalence.
No converse claim is made: the bijection sigma with e_i=f_sigma(i) is asserted outright rather than as a reverse implication of an iff.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all eight steps and the ring definition: central products ef and e(1-f) are orthogonal idempotents, primitivity makes each intersection 0 or e, and nonzero orthogonal families yield injectivity and surjectivity. If either family is empty the ring is zero and both are empty. Finite indexing avoids AC; no semisimplicity or field assumption is used. No routed decision is owed for this unchanged unflagged carrier.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

**Permutation matrices and the monomial subgroup.** Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a
prime power, let $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with diagonal torus $T$ and
standard flag $V_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n$ as in
[[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]], and let
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ be the symmetric group of the set
$\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]], [[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]]),
so that permutations are composed as functions and an element $\sigma\in S_n$ is
written in one-line notation as the list $\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n)$.

For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **permutation matrix** $P_\sigma\in G$ is the matrix with
$$(P_\sigma)_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i=\sigma(j),\\0,&i\ne\sigma(j),\end{cases}$$
that is, the $j$-th column of $P_\sigma$ is the standard basis vector
$e_{\sigma(j)}$, so that the $j$-th column has its unique entry $1$ in row
$\sigma(j)$. In particular $P_{\mathrm{id}}=I_n$, and multiplying matrices gives
$$P_\sigma P_\tau=P_{\sigma\circ\tau}\qquad(\sigma,\tau\in S_n),$$
because the $(i,k)$ entry of $P_\sigma P_\tau$ is $\sum_j(P_\sigma)_{ij}(P_\tau)_{jk}$,
which is $1$ exactly when $j=\tau(k)$ and $i=\sigma(j)=\sigma(\tau(k))$, and $0$
otherwise. A matrix $m\in G$ is **monomial** when every row and every column of
$m$ has exactly one nonzero entry. The **monomial subgroup** of $G$ is
$$N:=\{\,m\in G:m\text{ is monomial}\,\}.$$
Every $m\in N$ has a unique expression
$$m=t\,P_\sigma,\qquad t=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in T,\quad\sigma\in S_n,$$
namely with $\sigma(j)$ the row of the nonzero entry of column $j$ and
$t_{\sigma(j)}$ that entry; conversely $tP_\sigma$ is monomial with nonzero
entries $t_i$ in the rows and columns determined by $\sigma$. Consequently
$$N=T\cdot\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in S_n\}=\{P_\sigma t':\sigma\in S_n,\ t'\in T\},$$
since diagonal matrices may be moved across a permutation matrix.
$N$ is a subgroup of $G$: it contains $I_n=P_{\mathrm{id}}$, the product
$m m'$ of monomial matrices is monomial because the unique nonzero entry of each
column of $m'$ is transported to a unique nonzero entry of the corresponding
column of $mm'$, and the inverse of a monomial matrix is monomial since
permuting and rescaling rows and columns can be undone. Moreover $T\le N$ and
$T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$.

**The Weyl group.** Define the **sign permutation** of a monomial matrix by
$$w:N\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad w(tP_\sigma):=\sigma,$$
which is well defined by the uniqueness of the decomposition. It is a group
homomorphism: if $m=tP_\sigma$ and $m'=t'P_\tau$, then
$t''':=P_\sigma t'P_\sigma^{-1}$ is diagonal, so
$mm'=t\,t'''\,P_\sigma P_\tau=t\,t'''\,P_{\sigma\tau}$ by
[[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], whence $w(mm')=\sigma\circ\tau=w(m)w(m')$.
Its kernel is exactly $T$, since $w(tP_\sigma)=\mathrm{id}$ says
$\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and then $tP_{\mathrm{id}}=t$. Being a surjective
homomorphism, $w$ has kernel $T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$ by
[[def-normal-subgroup]], and the induced map on cosets
$$W:=N/T\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad mT\longmapsto w(m),$$
is well defined (left multiplication by an element of $T=\ker w$ does not change
$w$) and is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse $\sigma\mapsto P_\sigma T$;
here $N/T$ is the quotient group of [[def-quotient-group]]. We call
$$W=N/T\cong S_n$$
the **(split) Weyl group** of $G$. Note that $W$ is defined as a quotient of the
monomial subgroup $N$ and **not** as the quotient $N_G(T)/T$ of the normaliser
of $T$ inside $G$: at $q=2$ the torus $T$ is trivial and $N_G(T)/T$ is all of
$G$, while $N/T\cong S_n$ still holds. For $\sigma\in S_n$ we write $w_\sigma$ for
the class of $P_\sigma$ in $W$, so that $w_\sigma w_\tau=w_{\sigma\tau}$ and the
isomorphism above sends $w_\sigma$ to $\sigma$; we write $1:=w_{\mathrm{id}}$
for the identity of $W$.

**Simple reflections.** For $1\le i<n$ let $s_i:=(i\ i+1)\in S_n$ be the
adjacent transposition of $i$ and $i+1$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and put
$$\mathbf s_i:=w_{s_i}=P_{s_i}T\in W .$$
The elements $\mathbf s_1,\dots,\mathbf s_{n-1}$ are the **simple reflections** of
$W$; they generate $W$, because the adjacent transpositions generate $S_n$
([[thm-adjacent-transpositions-generate-the-symmetric-group]]) and $w$ is
surjective.

**Inversion length.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **inversion set** and **length**
are
$$\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma):=\{\,(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\,\}, \qquad \ell(\sigma):=\#\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma),$$
and for $w_\sigma\in W$ we set $\ell(w_\sigma):=\ell(\sigma)$, which is
well defined because every element of $W$ has the form $w_\sigma$ for exactly
one $\sigma$. Thus $\ell(1)=0$ and $\ell(w_{s_i})=1$ for every $i$, a single
inversion being created by the transposition of adjacent entries. Length is
invariant under inversion of the permutation: the map
$(i,j)\mapsto(\sigma(j),\sigma(i))$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma)$
to $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma^{-1})$ — if $i<j$ and $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$, then
setting $a:=\sigma(j)<b:=\sigma(i)$ gives $a<b$ while
$\sigma^{-1}(a)=j>i=\sigma^{-1}(b)$ — hence
$$\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w)\qquad(w\in W).$$
We stress that $\ell$ is here defined combinatorially as an inversion count and
that no Coxeter-theoretic description of it as a minimal word length is used on
this page.

**Parabolic Weyl subgroups.** Let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be a composition of
$n$ with blocks $I_1,\dots,I_r$ and standard parabolic $P_\alpha$ and Levi
$L_\alpha$ ([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]). The
**standard parabolic subgroup of $W$** attached to $\alpha$ is
$$W_\alpha:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(I_i)=I_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le r\,\},$$
the group of permutations preserving each block of $\alpha$ as a set; it is
isomorphic to $S_{a_1}\times\cdots\times S_{a_r}$ by restriction to the blocks,
and its elements are exactly the $\sigma$ whose length is the sum of the lengths
of the restrictions $\sigma|_{I_i}$. In terms of the monomial subgroup, a
monomial matrix lies in $P_\alpha$ exactly when its permutation matrix has
$\sigma(I_i)=I_i$ for all $i$, that is, exactly when $\sigma\in W_\alpha$;
consequently
$$N\cap P_\alpha=N\cap L_\alpha=T\cdot\{\,P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\,\}, \qquad W_\alpha=w(N\cap P_\alpha),$$
and $\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\}$ is a complement to $T$ in $N\cap P_\alpha$: its intersection with $T$ is $\{I_n\}$ and every element has the unique form $tP_\sigma$. The two extreme
cases are
$$W_{(n)}=S_n,\qquad W_{(1^n)}=\{1\},$$
corresponding to $P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$ and to $P_{(1^n)}=B$ with $L_{(1^n)}=T$
and $W_{(1^n)}=w(T)=\{1\}$: the single block of $(n)$ is preserved by every
permutation, while each singleton block of $(1^n)$ must be fixed, so only the
identity survives.

For a set $X$, let

$$X^*:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}X^n$$

be the set of finite words in letters from $X$, where $X^n$ is the set of functions $n\to X$. With concatenation and the empty word, $X^*$ is a monoid. The one-letter map $i_X:X\to X^*$ has the universal property that every function $u:X\to M$ into a monoid extends uniquely to a monoid homomorphism $\widehat u:X^*\to M$.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

The quotient ring $R/I$ with $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$.

Let $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$.  Since $I$ is an additive subgroup of the
abelian group $(R,+)$, its additive cosets form the quotient group $R/I$
([[def-quotient-group]], [[cor-subgroups-of-abelian-groups-are-normal]]).  Define

$$(r+I)(s+I):=rs+I.$$

The well-definedness and ring laws are established by
[[thm-quotient-ring-multiplication-well-defined-iff-ideal]] and
[[thm-quotient-ring-laws]].

derivations.claim: Put $X:=\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ and $F:=R^{(X^*)}$, the free $R$-module with the finite words in $X$ as basis [F5]; write the basis word corresponding to $i_1,\dots,i_k$ as $T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$ and the empty word as $1$. Extending concatenation of words $R$-bilinearly makes $F$ a unital associative $R$-algebra: concatenation is associative with two-sided identity the empty word by [F4], and distributivity holds by the bilinear extension. Let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated by the relators $r_i:=T_i^2-(q-1)T_i-q\cdot1$, $b_i:=T_iT_{i+1}T_i-T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ and $d_{ij}:=T_iT_j-T_jT_i$, and put $H:=F/I$, which by [F1] is the presented algebra $H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the image of $T_i$ being again written $T_i$; every element of $H$ is the image of an $R$-linear combination of words in the $T_i$, so $H$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$.

Define $\rho:F\to F$ on the word basis by $\rho(T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}):=T_{i_k}\cdots T_{i_1}$ and $\rho(1):=1$, extended $R$-linearly. Then $\rho$ is an $R$-linear involution and reverses products, $\rho(xy)=\rho(y)\rho(x)$, because reversal of a concatenation is the concatenation of the reversals in the opposite order and both sides are $R$-bilinear; in particular $\rho^2=\mathrm{id}_F$ and $\rho(T_i)=T_i$ for each generator.

$\rho$ preserves $I$, i.e. $\rho(I)\subseteq I$: the relators are fixed up to sign, $\rho(r_i)=r_i$, $\rho(b_i)=b_i$ and $\rho(d_{ij})=-d_{ij}$ by step 1.2, so each lies in $I$; the set $J:=\{x\in F:\rho(x)\in I\}$ contains $0$, is closed under addition and additive inverses because $\rho$ is $R$-linear and $I$ is an additive subgroup, and for $x\in J$ and $a\in F$ one has $\rho(ax)=\rho(x)\rho(a)\in I$ and $\rho(xa)=\rho(a)\rho(x)\in I$ because $I$ is a two-sided ideal [F6]; hence $J$ is a two-sided ideal containing all relators, so $(S)\subseteq J$ and $I=(S)\subseteq J$, that is, $\rho(I)\subseteq I$.

Consequently $\bar\rho:H\to H$, $\bar\rho(x+I):=\rho(x)+I$, is well defined: if $x-y\in I$ then $\rho(x)-\rho(y)=\rho(x-y)\in I$ by step 2.1. It is an $R$-linear anti-automorphism of $H$ with $\bar\rho^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\bar\rho(T_i)=T_i$: the quotient operations of [F7] and step 1.2 give $\bar\rho((x+I)(y+I))=\rho(xy)+I=\rho(y)\rho(x)+I=\bar\rho(y+I)\bar\rho(x+I)$, and similarly for addition, scalars and the unit.

$\bar\rho$ is the unique $R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $\bar\rho(T_i)=T_i$ for all $i$: if $\alpha$ is any such anti-automorphism, then $\alpha$ and $\bar\rho$ agree on $1$, and for a word $T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$ one has $\alpha(T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k})=\alpha(T_{i_k})\cdots\alpha(T_{i_1})=T_{i_k}\cdots T_{i_1}=\bar\rho(T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k})$; the words span $H$ by step 1.1, so $\alpha=\bar\rho$ by $R$-linearity.

For $w\in S_n$ and a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one has $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}$ in the generic algebra and hence $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H$; thus $T_w^*=\bar\rho(T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell})=T_{i_\ell}\cdots T_{i_1}$ by step 3.1. The reversed word $s_{i_\ell}\cdots s_{i_1}$ represents $w^{-1}$ and has $\ell$ letters, and $\ell=\ell(w)=\ell(w^{-1})$ by [F3], so it is a reduced expression of $w^{-1}$ and therefore $T_{w^{-1}}=T_{i_\ell}\cdots T_{i_1}\in H$; hence $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w$, and $T_w$ is well defined in $H$ independently of the chosen reduced expression by [F1] and [F2].

The assertions of the statement follow: $*:=\bar\rho$ is the unique extension of the assignment $T_i\mapsto T_i$, an involution by step 3.1; $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ is step 4.2; therefore $(T_wT_{w^{-1}})^*=T_{w^{-1}}^*T_w^*=T_{(w^{-1})^{-1}}T_{w^{-1}}=T_wT_{w^{-1}}$; and for the parabolic subgroup $S_\lambda$ the map $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ is a bijection of $S_\lambda$, so $m_\lambda^*=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_{w^{-1}}=\sum_{v\in S_\lambda}T_v=m_\lambda$. No choice principle is used: the constructions are explicit on the word basis.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: The submodules $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ and $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ are two-sided ideals of $A$, and the following two congruence rules hold modulo $A^{\rhd\lambda}$: for all $a\in A$ and $u,v\in T(\lambda)$, $$c^{\lambda}_{us}a\equiv\sum_{w\in T(\lambda)}r_w\,c^{\lambda}_{uw},\qquad a\,c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\sum_{w\in T(\lambda)}s_w\,c^{\lambda}_{wv},$$ where the $r_w$ do not depend on $u$ and the $s_w$ do not depend on $v$. Indeed, the first is the cellular rule [F1] applied to the fixed label $\lambda$, the second-slot index $s$ and the element $a$, which gives coefficients independent of the free first index $u$; right multiplication by $a$ therefore preserves each $A^{\unrhd\mu}$ and $A^{\rhd\mu}$, so $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ and (as its span over all $\mu\rhd\lambda$) $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ are right ideals, while applying the anti-automorphism $i$ to the first rule — it swaps the two indices, fixes $R$ and preserves both spans — gives the second rule and shows that they are also left ideals.

Existence and uniqueness of the form: for all $s,t\in T(\lambda)$ there is a unique $r=r(s,t)\in R$ with $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv r\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ for all $u,v$, and $r$ depends only on $s,t$. Since $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ is a two-sided ideal by step 1.1, the quotient ring $A/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ contains $Q:=A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ with $R$-basis the classes $\bar c_{uv}:=c^{\lambda}_{uv}+A^{\rhd\lambda}$. Applying the two rules of step 1.1 to the product $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}$ — first with $a:=c^{\lambda}_{tv}$, then with $a:=c^{\lambda}_{us}$ — gives $$\bar c_{us}\bar c_{tv}=\sum_w\rho_w\bar c_{uw}=\sum_x\sigma_x\bar c_{xv},$$ where $\rho_w$ does not depend on $u$ and $\sigma_x$ does not depend on $v$. Comparing the coefficients of $\bar c_{ab}$ in the two bases: the left expansion contributes $\rho_b$ when $a=u$ and $0$ otherwise, the right expansion $\sigma_a$ when $b=v$ and $0$ otherwise; hence $\sigma_a=0$ for $a\ne u$ and $\rho_b=0$ for $b\ne v$, leaving $\bar c_{us}\bar c_{tv}=\sigma_u\bar c_{uv}=\rho_v\bar c_{uv}$. The common value $\sigma_u=\rho_v$ is independent of $v$ (being $\sigma_u$) and independent of $u$ (being $\rho_v$), so it depends only on $s,t$; call it $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$. It is determined by the displayed congruence, because the coefficient of $\bar c_{uv}$ in the indicated free basis is unique, including over the zero ring. Bilinear extension gives the unique $R$-bilinear form with the stated property.

Symmetry: for all $s,t,u,v$, using that $i$ is an anti-automorphism with $i(c^{\lambda}_{ab})=c^{\lambda}_{ba}$, fixes $R$ and preserves $A^{\rhd\lambda}$, one has $$\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}\equiv c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}=(c^{\lambda}_{vt}c^{\lambda}_{su})^{i}\equiv\bigl(\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_{vu}\bigr)^{i}=\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv},$$ so $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda$, and by bilinearity $\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$ for all $x,y\in C^{\lambda}$.

Associativity: fix $s,t\in T(\lambda)$ and $a\in A$, and write $c^{\lambda}_s a=\sum_wr_wc^{\lambda}_w$ in $C^{\lambda}$ — the coefficients $r_w$ are those of step 1.1. Then, by step 2.1 applied first to $c^{\lambda}_sa$ and bilinearity of the form, $$\langle c^{\lambda}_sa,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\sum_wr_w\bar c_{uw}\bar c_{tv}=(\bar c_{us}\bar a)\cdot\bar c_{tv}=\bar c_{us}\cdot\bigl(\bar a\bar c_{tv}\bigr).$$ The second rule of step 1.1 writes $ac^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\sum_xs_xc^{\lambda}_{xv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ with coefficients $s_x$ characterised by $c^{\lambda}_ti(a)=\sum_xs_xc^{\lambda}_x$ in $C^{\lambda}$; hence $$\bar c_{us}\cdot\bigl(\bar a\bar c_{tv}\bigr)=\sum_xs_x\bar c_{us}\bar c_{xv}=\sum_xs_x\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_x\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_ti(a)\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}.$$ Cancelling the basis element $\bar c_{uv}$ gives $\langle c^{\lambda}_sa,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,i(a)c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$; by bilinearity this is $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $x,y\in C^{\lambda}$. Replacing $a$ by $i(a)$ and using $i^2=\mathrm{id}$ gives the equivalent left-action form $\langle x\,i(a),y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)\cdot y\rangle_\lambda$, where $i(a)\cdot y=y\,i(i(a))=y\,a$ is the left action of $i(a)$: this is the dual statement.

The adjointness identity $x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$ holds for all $x\in C^{\lambda}$ and $u,v\in T(\lambda)$: it suffices to treat $x=c^{\lambda}_s$, and there step 2.1 with $(u,s,t,v):=(s,s,u,v)$ gives $c^{\lambda}_{ss}c^{\lambda}_{uv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$; by the definition of the right action in [F1], the coefficients of $c^{\lambda}_{sv}$ on the right are exactly the coefficients of $c^{\lambda}_v$ in $c^{\lambda}_s\cdot c^{\lambda}_{uv}$, so $c^{\lambda}_s\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$; bilinearity in $x$ extends this to all $x$.

The radical is a submodule and a kernel: for fixed $y\in C^{\lambda}$ the assignment $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda$ is an $R$-linear map with kernel $\{x:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\}$, so $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}=\bigcap_y\ker(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda)$ is an $R$-submodule; and if $x\in\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ then for every $a\in A$ and $y\in C^{\lambda}$ step 3.2 gives $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda=0$, so $xa\in\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$: the radical is an $A$-submodule, namely the kernel of the $A$-module map $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$. This completes the proof of (i)-(iv).

citations.quote:
In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

For every commutative ring $R$ with invertible parameter $z$, the ordinary
finite type-A Hecke algebra $H_n$ and a composition $\rho$ of $n$, the
permutation module $x_\rho H_n$ has $R$-basis
$$m_{(S,t)}=\sum_{s:\,\rho(s)=S}m_{st},$$
where $S$ ranges over the semistandard tableaux of partition shape and type
$\rho$ and $t$ over the standard tableaux of the same shape. It has a Specht
filtration with multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$ of the
ordinary Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). The row-double-coset
membership uses each coset word once and no quantum-factorial division. Over
the generic field this number equals the trivial-character multiplicity of the
$\rho$-row parabolic in $S^\lambda$. Moreover the explicit ordinary Garnir
row-coset identity, the additive nonstandard-tableau factorization and the
same-column generator refinement
$$T_am_{st}\equiv-m_{st}+\sum_{u\lhd s}c_um_{ut}\pmod{\text{higher shapes}}$$
hold; row-standard straightening has no smaller-shape terms and its same-shape
terms increase tableau-prefix dominance. Shape support uses the already proved
ordinary Murphy dominance ideals
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]); the finite Garnir
algorithm terminates in lexicographic shape/tableau order before that
dominance refinement.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape
$\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection
$$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$
We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$
as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry. Thus a tableau
places each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ in exactly one node of $[\lambda]$. For
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the diagram is empty and the empty map is the unique
tableau of shape $\varnothing$, the **empty tableau**. The **shape** of a
tableau $t$ is the partition $\lambda$ with $t:[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$,
which is determined by $t$ because $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$.

**Standard tableaux.** A tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is **standard** if its
entries strictly increase along rows and down columns, that is, if
$$t(i,j)<t(i,j+1)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i,j+1)\in[\lambda],$$
$$t(i,j)<t(i+1,j)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i+1,j)\in[\lambda].$$
The empty tableau is standard, because both conditions are vacuous, and it is
the unique standard tableau of shape $\varnothing$. Following the classical
notation we write $f^\lambda$ for the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux.

**The left action on tableaux.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a $\lambda$-tableau
$t$, define
$$(\sigma\cdot t)(i,j):=\sigma\bigl(t(i,j)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((i,j)\in[\lambda]\bigr).$$
Since $t$ is a bijection onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\sigma$ is a bijection of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the map $\sigma\cdot t$ is again a bijection
$[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, hence again a $\lambda$-tableau, and
$\mathrm{id}\cdot t=t$, $\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot t)=(\sigma\tau)\cdot t$ for all
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$: the rule is a left action of $S_n$ on the set of
$\lambda$-tableaux. For every $\sigma\in S_n$ the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
are the images under $\sigma$ of the row sets of $t$, and the column sets of
$\sigma\cdot t$ are the images under $\sigma$ of the column sets of $t$.

For every $n\ge0$,
$$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$
where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and
$f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series. The zero module has the empty series and length $0$.
Any two composition series of a module have the same length, and their simple factors agree up to permutation and isomorphism. See [[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]].

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series. The zero module has the empty series and length $0$.
Any two composition series of a module have the same length, and their simple factors agree up to permutation and isomorphism. See [[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]].

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$,
with diagrams $[\lambda]$ and $[\mu]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For content counts
only, set $\mu_i:=0$ for $i$ beyond the number of parts of $\mu$; these
zeros are not additional parts of the partition.

A **semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$**, also called a
semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and **type $\mu$**, is a filling
$T:[\lambda]\to\{1,2,\dots\}$ of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ with positive
integers such that:

1. **content:** for every $i\ge 1$ the entry $i$ occurs in exactly $\mu_i$
   boxes of $[\lambda]$, so the multiset of entries is
   $\{1^{\mu_1},2^{\mu_2},\dots\}$ and in particular every entry lies between
   $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$;
2. **rows:** the entries weakly increase along every row, that is,
   $T(i,j)\le T(i,j+1)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i,j+1)$ are both in
   $[\lambda]$;
3. **columns:** the entries strictly increase down every column, that is,
   $T(i,j)<T(i+1,j)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i+1,j)$ are both in $[\lambda]$.

The **Kostka number** $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is the number of semistandard
tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$:
$$K_{\lambda,\mu}:=\#\{\,T:T\text{ is a semistandard }\lambda\text{-tableau of content }\mu\,\}.$$
This is well defined and finite: a filling of the $n$ boxes of $[\lambda]$ by
positive integers has at most $n^n$ possibilities for $n\ge1$ once each entry is required
to lie between $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$, and conditions 1--3 cut this
finite set down to the semistandard tableaux, so $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is a
nonnegative integer. It is zero when the conditions cannot be met.

Two entries may be equal inside a row, but never inside a column: a repeated
entry in a column would contradict the strict increase of condition 3, so the
repetitions of a label forced by the content $\mu$ must be spread across
distinct columns of $[\lambda]$. For $\lambda=\mu=\varnothing$ there is a
single filling, the empty one, so
$$K_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=1 .$$

**Relation to standard tableaux.** Because a tableau of content $(1^n)$ uses
each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, its entries are pairwise
distinct, and weak increase along a row is then strict increase along that
row; a filling of $[\lambda]$ with content $(1^n)$ is therefore semistandard
exactly when it is a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]), that is,
$$K_{\lambda,(1^n)}=f^\lambda ,$$
the number of standard tableaux of shape $\lambda$. In particular, for $n\ge1$,
$K_{(n),(1^n)}=K_{(n),(n)}=1$, since the single row carries either the
standard entries $1,2,\dots,n$ or the $n$ copies of the entry $1$, and
$K_{(1^n),(1^n)}=1$, realized by the single column $1,2,\dots,n$ read from
top to bottom.

For every $d\ge0$ and partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash d$,
$$h_\mu=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}K_{\lambda\mu}s_\lambda.$$
Moreover, $K_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, and
$K_{\mu\mu}=1$. Thus, after ordering the partitions of $d$ by any linear
extension of dominance from smaller to larger, the matrix
$(K_{\lambda\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}$ is lower unitriangular over
$\mathbb Z$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.
Any two composition series of a module have the same length, and their simple factors agree up to permutation and isomorphism. See [[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]].

Right multiplication by $p$ is a linear projection, and preserves every $S$-submodule, although it need not be an $S$-linear endomorphism when $p$ is not central. Taking dimensions proves additivity. Only the canonical partition weight projections are used.
