Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For prime $e=p$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]; the same inequalities define the
extension to composite finite $e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a

Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: Reconstruct a tableau from its residue tuple. At a prefix of size $k-1$, two different addable corners have integer content difference of absolute value at most $k$. Since $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ and $e>n$, their q-contents differ. Starting with the empty diagram, the tuple thus recovers each added node and the final shape. For two tableaux of a fixed shape with identical entries' residues outside $i,i+1$, first reconstruct the common prefix through $i-1$, and reconstruct the common suffix by successively deleting the unique appropriate removable corner from the fixed final shape. The intervening skew diagram has two boxes; its only possible orders are the original order and its swap. This proves both separation assertions.

Diagonalize the commuting JM operators on a cell. Their triangular basis gives a filtration with one-dimensional joint characters indexed by standard tableaux. Those characters are distinct by step 1.1. For commuting triangular operators, the simultaneous generalized eigenspaces split along their distinct joint characters: the corresponding maximal ideals of the polynomial algebra are pairwise comaximal. Each joint character occurs once in this cell, so each generalized eigenspace is one-dimensional and hence an actual joint eigenline. This finite Chinese-remainder argument works over any field and needs no choice of a generic scalar or algebraic closure. The Lagrange product of the Statement is $1$ on its target tuple and $0$ on every other tuple. Applied to $m_t$, its triangular diagonal coefficient is $1$, and the other possible terms are strictly more dominant. Thus it gives the asserted $f_t$.

Compute the diagonal coefficient using the **correctly ordered** JM relation $$T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(q-1)L_{i+1}-1.$$ For $k\ne i,i+1$, $T_i$ commutes with $L_k$. Consequently separation restricts $f_sT_i$ to the span of $f_s$ and $f_t$ if the swap is standard, or to $f_s$ alone otherwise. Write its coefficient of $f_s$ as $c_s$. The displayed relation gives $$c_s\bigl([\operatorname{content}_s(i)]_q-              [\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q\bigr)    =-(q-1)[\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q-1.$$ Its denominator is $q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}[\rho]_q$, while the numerator is $-q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}$, so $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. This does not claim that $T_i$ commutes with $L_i$.

At this stage step 2.1 establishes the projector identities on each individual cell module. The global identities in $H$ will follow below after proving that the sum of the cell modules is faithful. No finite-$e$ classification is a premise.

The transition from $m_t$ to $f_t$ is unitriangular, so these vectors form a basis. For $s\ne t$, choose $k$ at which their q-contents differ. Self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$ and associativity give $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q-    [\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)\langle f_s,f_t\rangle=0.$$ The scalar is nonzero, proving orthogonality. The Lagrange action also gives $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$.

If the swap is not standard, the consecutive entries lie adjacently in one row or one column. Then $\rho=-1$ or $\rho=1$, respectively, and step 2.2 gives $c_s=q$ or $c_s=-1$. These are the stated row and column cases; the row action is $q$, not the scalar $1$ at a general parameter.

Suppose the swap is standard. In the branch $s\rhd t$, the length-additive Murphy action has leading term $m_sT_i=m_t$; the unitriangular eigenbasis change then gives the off-diagonal coefficient $\alpha_i(s)=1$. Higher-dominance terms cannot alter the coefficient at $t$ in this two-dimensional eigenline span. This is the leading-term argument in Mathas's source theorem on the seminormal basis. In both branches the quadratic relation gives $$\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=q+(q-1)c_s-c_s^2  =\frac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q}.$$ The last equality follows directly from $[-\rho]_q=-q^{-\rho}[\rho]_q$ and the quantum-integer addition identities. Thus the opposite branch has exactly the displayed coefficient. This proves the generator formula without accepting the inconsistent branch in the 1998 manuscript.

Prove nondegeneracy in the separated range locally. The canonical Murphy basis vector has form value $[\lambda]!_q=\prod_a[\lambda_a]!_q$, because $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_qx_\lambda$; its seminormal image has the same value since the canonical tableau is dominance-maximal. This scalar is nonzero when $e>n$. If $s\rhd t=s(i,i+1)$ is a standard swap, put $a=1/[\rho]_q$. Step 4.1 gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+a)$. Associativity, orthogonality and the quadratic relation give $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(q+a)(1-a)\langle f_s,f_s\rangle=q[\rho+1]_q[\rho-1]_q[\rho]_q^{-2}\langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. Indeed expansion of $(T_i+a)^2$ and its $f_s$ coefficient $-a$ gives $q-a(q-1)-a^2=(q+a)(1-a)$. The swapped incomparable boxes have $2\le|\rho|\le n-1$: their row and column separations plus one are at most the size of the diagram. Thus all three quantum integers here are nonzero. Every standard tableau is connected to the canonical one by length-increasing swaps of adjacent incomparable entries: bubble-sort its linear extension of the box-order poset into the canonical row-order extension, then reverse the swaps. Induction gives nonzero diagonal norm at every $f_t$, so each cell form is nonsingular.

Each cell is now its nonzero simple form quotient, absolutely simple, and all these cells are pairwise distinct and exhaust the simple modules by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. Thus the split semisimple quotient $H/J(H)$ has dimension $\sum_\lambda |\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|^2$. This equals $\dim H$ because the Murphy cellular basis has exactly one element for each pair of standard tableaux of the same shape ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]). Hence $J(H)=0$, $H$ is split semisimple, and the direct sum of all its simple cell modules is faithful. On that faithful module the global Lagrange products of the Statement are the orthogonal projectors from step 2.1, with different shapes having disjoint tuples by step 1.1. Therefore $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_t$ holds in $H$ itself, proving the global idempotents. This argument proves only the separated range and does not assert a finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion when $e\le n$.

Steps 1.1-6.1 prove all four claims. No semisimplicity was imposed as a hypothesis: it was derived locally from nondegenerate cells and their complete finite-cell classification. The calculation concerns the intrinsic Murphy cell and keeps the signed ordinary-module dictionary separate. All products and basis changes are finite, and no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Statement part 2 uses global content sets over all shapes: a cell with one tableau need not have F_t=1 in H. For n=0 or 1 there is only one global tableau and the projector is 1. Steps 2.1 and 6.1 establish the global/cell distinction.
The denominators of F_t are nonzero exactly by part 1 (step 1.1), and part 4's term -1/[rho]_q is legitimate because |rho|<=n-1<e; step 5.1 records that no semisimplicity is assumed.
The projector f_t=m_t+sum over s strictly dominating t of a_s m_s has the single leading term m_t, and step 4.1 computes the generator action for t=s(i i+1) directly.
Degenerate residue collisions are excluded by the hypothesis e>n: step 1.1 shows distinct same-residue nodes share neither a row nor a column and distinct removable nodes have distinct residues.

boundaries.reason: The parameter e satisfies e>n (infinity allowed) and the remaining data are finite sets of standard tableaux; no interval, limiting process or extremal endpoint occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement's final sentence records that no choice principle is used; the construction lives in the commutative algebra F[L_1,...,L_n] generated by the fixed elements L_k.

boundaries.reason: The theorem's four parts are separation, a projector construction, orthogonality and a generator formula; none is the forward half of a biconditional.
No converse is claimed; in particular the theorem does not assert that equality in the generator formula characterises the seminormal projectors.

risk_review.notes: Contract-only enrichment. Reviewed all ten steps: addable-corner differences at prefix k are <=k, so e>n reconstructs the entire tuple, across shapes too; deleting removable corners proves the two-exception assertion. Distinct joint characters and finite comaximal primary ideals make the triangular commuting action a sum of actual one-dimensional eigenspaces, so no finite-field generic-scalar choice is used. The correctly ordered JM relation gives c_s=-1/[rho]_q; one branch has leading coefficient 1 and the quadratic relation fixes the opposite coefficient. Norm propagation is (q+a)(1-a), with 2<=|rho|<=n-1 for incomparable swaps, giving nonzero forms. Classification and the semisimple-quotient/Wedderburn interfaces (already read in the JM supplier prerequisites) then make the sum of the cells faithful, upgrading global-content Lagrange operators to idempotents in H. Empty/singleton n, q=1 and positive-characteristic fields meet the same e>n condition. This proof does not require the unresolved finite-e classification for e<=n.

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID,
$\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose
extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $\nu_\pi$ be
the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $\nu_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let
$G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any
$R$-basis of $M$. Then
$$\nu_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$
where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of
[[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is
finite and independent of the chosen basis.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$(q-1)[m]_q=q^m-1$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. When $q-1$ is a unit this
may be written $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$; the polynomial definition requires no
such division. Also $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the

([[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]],

([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each

characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$(q-1)[m]_q=q^m-1$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. When $q-1$ is a unit this
may be written $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$; the polynomial definition requires no
such division. Also $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
isomorphism given by the Coxeter presentation and the standard bases
([[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) — sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

derivations.claim: Cell $(2,1)$: $S_{(2,1)}=\langle s_1\rangle$, so $m_{(2,1)}=1+T_1$; the two standard tableaux of shape $(2,1)$ are $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ (row reading word $1\,2\,3$, so $d(t)=1$) and $u=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ (row reading word $1\,3\,2$, so $d(u)=s_2$). Hence $m_{tt}=1\cdot(1+T_1)\cdot1=1+T_1$, $m_{tu}=(1+T_1)T_2$, $m_{ut}=T_2^*(1+T_1)=T_2(1+T_1)$ and $m_{uu}=T_2^*(1+T_1)T_2=T_2(1+T_1)T_2$, using $T_2^*=T_2$ and $m_{(2,1)}^*=m_{(2,1)}$.

Cells $(3)$ and $(1^3)$: $S_{(3)}=S_3$ has six elements with reduced expressions $1,s_1,s_2,s_1s_2,s_2s_1,s_1s_2s_1$, so $m_{(3)}=1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1=T_{d(s)}^*m_{(3)}T_{d(s)}$ for the unique standard tableau; $S_{(1^3)}$ is trivial, so its group algebra sum is the identity, $m_{(1^3)}=1$, and $m_{vv}=1$.

Count and anti-involution: the three cells contribute $1^2+2^2+1^2=6=3!=|S_3|$ elements, in agreement with $H$ being free of rank $6$; and $m_{tu}^*=m_{ut}$ is the instance of the general identity $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ of [F1], the middle cell being the one with two indices.
Specialization: setting $q=1$ turns $T_w$ into $w$, so the displayed elements become the Murphy basis of $R[S_3]$; this is the $n=3$ case of [F3].

The trivial-cell computation of step 1.2 uses the group-algebra sum over the trivial subgroup, m_{(1^3)}=1, and no vanishing coefficient is silently dropped anywhere in the displayed products.

boundaries.reason: There is no interval or limiting parameter; the example computes one finite basis of a rank-six algebra over an arbitrary commutative ring.
Every sum runs over the finite symmetric group S_3 or one of its subgroups and every tableau is displayed, so no family is selected and no choice principle enters.
The example exhibits a basis and verifies the cellular identities; it asserts no biconditional, so no forward direction is owed.
No converse claim occurs; the specialization at q=1 is applied to the displayed elements rather than used as one side of an equivalence.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $
u$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^
u$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^
u]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Fix a beta length $L\ge1$. For a partition $
u$ with at most $L$ columns (that is, $
u_1\le L$), put $$ eta_i(
u)=
u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. Negative entries remain negative after decrementing. Thus the identity also holds in all zero-symbol cases. At $\mu=0$ its value is the sorting sign for a permutation of $(L-1,\ldots,0)$ and is zero otherwise, so the recursion terminates without another unproved extension rule.

In the formulas of this page take $L=r$ when $r>0$. A nonzero degree-$r$ partition has width at most $r$, so this length suffices; the Weyl cutoff $\ell(
u)\le d$ is retained even when $d<r$. A balanced displacement $+h\mathbf e_b-h\mathbf e_c$ preserves total degree. An unbalanced change is not silently treated as a class in the same fixed-degree group. The empty degree is handled by the empty beta sequence and unit symbol. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^	imes$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. Set $e_q=e(k,q)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda^+(d,n)$ let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module with Schur cell form $B_\lambda$ and nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Write $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for the independent Murphy cell module and its cell-form quotient ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal F(W^\lambda)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ as right $H$-modules, and this isomorphism identifies $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}$ exactly with the Murphy cell form. 2. $\mathcal F(L^\lambda)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including the zero quotient; it is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e_q$-restricted. 3. For every $e_q$-restricted $
u\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^
u]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(
u)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^	heta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^	heta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $
u$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{
u'}]=[S^\lambda:D^
u].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $\lambda\vdash n$
with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, and let $H$, $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$,
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_\mu$, the
permutation form $\beta$ and the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. Write
$b_r:=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}$ for the row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $r$
(the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$) and
$$e_t:=z_\lambda T_{d_\mu(t)}\in P(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)).$$
For row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $u,v$ write $u\le v$ when for all
$m,k\ge1$ the first $k$ rows of $u$ contain at most as many labels $\le m$ as
the first $k$ rows of $v$, and let $t'$ be the transpose of $t$, a standard
$\lambda$-tableau. Then:

1. $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, so
   $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$, and
   the inclusion $P(\lambda)\subseteq M(\lambda)$ splits as a map of
   $R$-modules.

2. For every $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$ one has, with coefficients
   $a_{r,t}\in R$,
   $$e_t=q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}\,b_{t'}+\sum_{r<t'}a_{r,t}\,b_r,$$
   where the sum runs over the row-standard $r$ with $r\le t'$, $r\ne t'$; the
   square minor with rows $\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is therefore
   triangular with respect to any linear extension of the order $\le$ on
   $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$, with diagonal entries
   $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$, all units of $R$.

3. The Gram matrix of the DJ form in the basis $\{e_t\}$ is
   $$B_{tu}=\sum_{r}a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}\qquad(t,u\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)),$$
   where $a_{r,t}$ denotes the full coefficient of $b_r$ in $e_t$: it is $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$ for $r=t'$, the displayed lower coefficient for $r<t'$, and zero otherwise. Unit triangularity is a property of the
   embedding, not of the Gram matrix: $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may be degenerate.

4. Let $(i,j)$ be a Garnir node of $\mu$, that is, a node of $\mu$ with
   $j\le\mu_{i+1}$, put
   $\alpha=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{i-1},j-1,\mu_i+1,\mu_{i+1}-j,\mu_{i+2},\dots)$
   with zero parts deleted and $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\mu$, and let
   $\theta(T_d)\in H$ be the product of the elements
   $\theta(T_r)=(q-1)-T_r$ over a reduced word of $d$
   ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Then
   $$z_\lambda\sum_{d\in D}\theta(T_d)=0\qquad\text{in }P(\lambda).$$
   The coefficients are determined by the finite coset identity of step 2.2 and
   survive every base change; together with the unit minor of clause 2 these
   relations give a finite straightening of the elements $z_\lambda T_w$ to
   the standard basis $\{e_t\}$.

5. Every clause is compatible with the base change
   $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$. The proof
   uses no generic semisimplicity, divides by no quantum factorial and uses no
   choice principle.

derivations.claim: Check the lift. Localization makes $\hat q$ a unit since its residue is $-1$, so the exact PID hypotheses of [F1] hold; the generic factorial is nonzero. The identities $[2]=1+\hat q$, $[4]=(1+\hat q)(1+\hat q^2)$ and evaluation of the odd quantum integers at $-1$ prove [F2]. These values refer to this lift, not an arbitrary field or lift with quantum characteristic $2$.

Compute the balanced symbols explicitly. For $(3,2)$, $\beta=(6,5,3,1,0)$ and its hook array is $\begin{smallmatrix}4&3&1\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}$. The pair $(1,1),(1,2)$ gives $(9,2,3,1,0)$, which sorts to the beta sequence of $(1^5)$ with sign $-1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(3)=1$. The pair $(1,1),(1,3)$ gives $(7,5,2,1,0)$, shape $(2,2,1)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(1)=1$. The pair $(2,1),(2,2)$ gives $(7,4,3,1,0)$, shape $(3,1^2)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(2)-v(1)=1$. The remaining pair has repeated beta entries and vanishes. Thus the first displayed Weyl identity follows by direct substitution.

Verify the two zero forms directly at $q=-1$. For each $\eta\in\{(3,2),(3,1,1)\}$, write $v_j$ for the Murphy vector whose row-reading word is, respectively, $12345,12435,12534,13425,13524$ for $j=0,\ldots,4$; the shape $(3,1,1)$ has the additional word $14523$, giving $v_5$. The row action gives $v_0T_1=v_0T_2=-v_0$, $v_1T_2=v_3$ and $v_2T_2=v_4$. The first-column Garnir belt between the first two rows gives $v_3T_1=-v_0-v_1-v_3$: its row-standard terms have lower first entry $1,2,3,4$, and its other side has shape $(4,1)$, strictly above either $\eta$. Also $v_3T_4=v_4$, $v_1T_4=v_2$ and $v_0T_4=-v_0$. The last identity is the row action for $(3,2)$; for $(3,1,1)$ it follows from $x_{(3,1,1)}(1+T_4)=x_{(3,2)}$, a higher-shape element. Since $T_1T_4=T_4T_1$, these identities give $v_4T_1=v_0-v_2-v_4$. These are finite row-action and Garnir calculations from the supplied integral Murphy construction.

Put $r_j=\langle v_0,v_j\rangle$. Self-adjointness of $T_1,T_2$ and $v_0T_i=-v_0$ imply $\langle v_0,v_jT_i\rangle=-r_j$. The four identities of step 1.3 consequently give $r_1=-r_0$, $r_2=r_0$, $r_3=-r_1$ and $r_4=-r_2$. But $r_0=[\eta]!_{-1}=0$, since $x_\eta^2=[\eta]!_q x_\eta$ and $[3]!_{-1}$ contains $[2]_{-1}=0$. Thus $r_0,\ldots,r_4$ are zero for both shapes.

Compute the smaller rows rather than assuming them. The same calculation for $(3,1^2)$ gives $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,1^2)}(i)]=[W^{(2,2,1)}]+[W^{(1^5)}]$: the pairs with hook lengths $(5,2)$ and $(2,1)$ give those two terms, while the $(5,1)$ coefficient is zero. For $(2,2,1)$, the only nonzero symbols arise from pairs $(4,2)$ and $(3,1)$, both of valuation difference zero. For $(2,1^3)$ the sole pair is $(5,1)$, also zero; $(1^5)$ has no pair. Hence these three Weyl modules have zero positive sums and zero radicals, so they equal their simple heads. For $(3,1^2)$ each displayed simple occurs once in the positive sum; because its first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it, both radical multiplicities are exactly $1$. Its class is consequently $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+[L^{(2,2,1)}]+[L^{(1^5)}]$. Substitution into step 1.2 now gives $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]$, proving the stated preliminary multiplicity conclusions without reading a signed individual Weyl coefficient as a simple multiplicity.

For the remaining vector of $(3,1,1)$, put $x=x_{(3,1,1)}$. Its distinguished inverse word is $T_3T_4T_2T_3$. Expanding the finite row symmetrizers with $T_i^2=-2T_i-1$ and the braid relations gives the exact identity $$xT_3T_4T_2T_3x=x_{(5)}-(1+T_4)x_{(4,1)}(1+T_4)-x_{(3,2)}.$$ Every term on the right belongs to the higher dominance ideal for $(3,1,1)$, so the cell-product coefficient is $r_5=0$. Together with step 2.1, this puts the canonical vector $v_0$ in the form radical of each cell. That radical is a submodule, and $v_0H$ is the entire Murphy cell, since its standard basis is $x_\eta T_{d(t)}$ modulo the higher ideal. Hence both forms are identically zero. Their Schur-simple images are zero by the exact radical-corner identity in [F3]. This uses no general Gram-entry divisor or finite-$e$ classification.

Supply the actual dimension argument. The regular-weight Gram product for the Murphy cell $(2,2,1)$ is $$\hat q^7\frac{[4]_{\hat q}}{[2]_{\hat q}}[3]_{\hat q}^4   =\hat q^7(1+\hat q^2)[3]_{\hat q}^4,$$ since its two signed symbols have shapes $(1^5)$ and $(2,1^3)$ with standard-tableau counts $1$ and $4$. The five standardizations have lengths $0,1,1,2,3$, giving exponent $7$. At $\hat q=-1$ this determinant is $-2\ne0$. Thus $S_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}=D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}$ is simple of dimension $5$, counted by its five standard tableaux. Both Schur simples $L^{(3,1^2)}$ and $L^{(3,2)}$ are killed by the local zero-form calculation of step 3.1 and the exact corner/form identity [F3]. Applying the functor to the positive sum of step 2.2 therefore gives $\sum_{i>0}[S_{\mathrm M}^{(3,2)}(i)]=2[D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}]$. The form of $(3,2)$ is identically zero by step 3.1, so its first submodule is the whole five-dimensional cell. Every composition factor of that cell must appear in the positive sum, hence must be this five-dimensional simple. Dimension forces exactly one factor, proving $S_{\mathrm M}^{(3,2)}\cong D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}$. Exact projection of a composition series, with distinct nonzero simple images as in [F3], gives $d_{(3,2),(2,2,1)}=1$.

A further consistency check is the regular-weight Gram product $\hat q^8[3]_{\hat q}[4]_{\hat q}^4[2]_{\hat q}^6$ for $(3,2)$, whose valuation is $10$, agreeing with two five-dimensional positive Specht submodules. This is a check of the complete balanced formula; it is not the unsupported full-hook product used in the former classification proof.

Translate simultaneously by $\theta$ and conjugation. The actual ordinary/Murphy module-and-form comparison sends the isomorphism of step 4.1 to $S_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(2,2,1)}\cong D_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(3,2)}$. The partition $(2,2,1)$ is not regular, so its own **cell-form quotient** is zero; this does not say its actual head is zero, since the module itself is simple. The dominance inequality $(3,2)\unrhd(2,2,1)$ agrees with the ordinary-convention unitriangular bound. This proves every claimed numeric conclusion.
