Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with

The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

derivations.claim: Work first over $A=\mathbb Z[u,u^{-1}]$ with fraction field $K=\mathbb Q(u)$. The regular trace pairing $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(\ell_{ab})$ has entries in $A$ in the standard Hecke basis. At $u=1$ its matrix is $n!\,\delta_{v,w^{-1}}$, so its determinant is nonzero and it is nondegenerate over $K$. If $a$ belongs to the Jacobson radical, $ab$ is nilpotent for every $b$ by [F4]; its left multiplication is nilpotent and has trace zero. Nondegeneracy forces the radical to vanish. Thus $H_K$ is semisimple. Its shape-$\lambda$ cell layer has the multiplication $XG_\lambda Y$ of [F1]. If $G_\lambda$ were singular, the nonzero subspace $\{X:G_\lambda X=0\}$ would be a two-sided ideal with square zero, contradicting [F4]. Hence $G_\lambda$ is invertible and $X\mapsto G_\lambda X$ identifies this layer with a full matrix algebra over $K$.

u$, the resulting map is zero on the other summands and sends $m_

u(t)=T}m_t$. Higher Schur maps with output type $\lambda$ have Hecke values of strictly dominant shape, so their output is killed by $\pi$. u(t)=T$ are disjoint. Each is nonempty: standardize equal entries of a semistandard tableau in increasing column order; equal entries cannot share a column, row order is retained, and different entries occupy disjoint consecutive label blocks. Hence their sums $m_T$ are independent in the free Murphy cell basis, over every $R$. This proves injectivity, including zero type entries. No surjectivity onto all specialized Hom spaces is asserted.

For an integral symmetric polynomial $f$, $z_f$ is central by [F2]. Its action on the generic cell layer is a bimodule endomorphism of that full matrix algebra, hence scalar: its value at the identity commutes with every matrix and the rest follows by multiplication. Accordingly its matrix on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)_K$ is scalar. The triangular matrices in [F2] give its diagonal as $f([c_t(1)]_u,\ldots,[c_t(n)]_u)$, equal to $a_\lambda(f)$ for every $t$ because $f$ is symmetric and the node multiset is fixed. Thus $z_f$ acts exactly by this scalar. Both sides have matrices over $A$, and injection into $K$ proves the identity before specialization. Every symmetric polynomial over an arbitrary $R$ is an $R$-linear combination of integral monomial symmetric polynomials: coefficients are constant on each monomial orbit. Apply the integral identities to these monomial polynomials and specialize $u\mapsto q$. Therefore every $z_f$ acts by $a_\lambda(f)$ on the actual Murphy cell over $R$, including singular parameters.

For central $z_f\in H$, right multiplication preserves every $M^\alpha$ and is $H$-linear. Every $H$-linear endomorphism $s$ of $M$ satisfies $s(mz_f)=s(m)z_f$, so $\rho_{z_f}$ is central in $S$. For $w\in W^\lambda$ and $m\in M$, step 1.2 and $H$-linearity give $$j(w\rho_{z_f})(m)=j(w)(mz_f)=j(w)(m)z_f=a_\lambda(f)j(w)(m),$$ the last equality by step 2.1. Injectivity gives $w\rho_{z_f}=a_\lambda(f)w$, proving the full ring-level assertion. If $M=0$ all cell assertions are empty. At rank zero the empty cell is $R$ with the empty polynomial evaluation, so the same conclusion holds.

Suppose now that $R=F$ and $L^\mu$ is a constituent of $W^\lambda$. Step 3.1 gives scalar $a_\lambda(f)$ on this constituent. Since $L^\mu$ is the nonzero quotient of $W^\mu$ by [F3], its scalar is also $a_\mu(f)$; hence they agree for every symmetric $f$. Taking all elementary symmetric polynomials gives $$\prod_{A\in[\lambda]}(X-[c(A)]_q)=\prod_{B\in[\mu]}(X-[c(B)]_q).$$ By [F5], if $q=1$ the distinct $e$ residues are the distinct prime-field values $[c]_1$; if $q\ne1$, $[a]_q=[b]_q$ is equivalent to $q^a=q^b$, hence to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Unique factorization of these monic products into distinct field-linear factors therefore gives equality of every residue multiplicity, also when the field characteristic divides a multiplicity. Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$ with $q$ an indeterminate, let $N\ge1$, and put $K_i=L_iL_{i+1}^{-1}$ for $1\le i<N$. Start with the free associative $F$-algebra on $L_j,L_j^{-1}$ ($1\le j\le N$) and $E_i,F_i$ ($1\le i<N$), and quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by the following relations:

1. $L_jL_j^{-1}=L_j^{-1}L_j=1$ and $L_jL_k=L_kL_j$ for all $j,k$.
2. $L_jE_iL_j^{-1}=q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}E_i$ and $L_jF_iL_j^{-1}=q^{-\delta_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i+1}}F_i$.
3. $[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$.
4. $[E_i,E_j]=[F_i,F_j]=0$ when $|i-j|>1$.
5. For $|i-j|=1$, $E_i^2E_j-(q+q^{-1})E_iE_jE_i+E_jE_i^2=0$ and $F_i^2F_j-(q+q^{-1})F_iF_jF_i+F_jF_i^2=0$.

Here $[x,y]=xy-yx$. The free algebra and quotient construction are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]; this definition asserts existence of the presented associative algebra, not the well-definedness of structural maps on its quotient.

On $V_N$ with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$, prescribe the candidate matrices
$$L_je_a=q^{\delta_{ja}}e_a,\qquad E_ie_a=\delta_{a,i+1}e_i,\qquad F_ie_a=\delta_{a,i}e_{i+1}.$$
Prescribe candidate coproduct and counit values by
$$\Delta(L_j)=L_j\otimes L_j,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i,$$
and $\epsilon(L_j^{\pm1})=1$, $\epsilon(E_i)=\epsilon(F_i)=0$. The following relation-descent lemma proves that these assignments define the vector representation and bialgebra structure, and hence the tensor actions used below.

lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, the algebra presentation and candidate maps in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]].

[F1] A free associative algebra modulo the two-sided ideal of its displayed relations is a presented algebra, and assignments descend exactly when they annihilate every defining relation ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]).

[F2] The tensor product of algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$, and maps agreeing on the displayed generators agree on the presented algebra ([[thm-tensor-product-of-algebras-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[lem-hh-universal-presentations-and-base-change]]).

[F3] For $a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{i+1,j}$, the defining $L$-weight relations imply $K_iE_jK_i^{-1}=q^{a_{ij}}E_j$ and $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q^{-a_{ij}}F_j$; in particular $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$, $a_{ii}=2$, and $a_{ij}=-1$ for adjacent indices.
lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 On $V_N$, each $L_j$ is diagonal and invertible, and the $L_j$ commute. Conjugating the matrix unit $E_i:e_{i+1}\mapsto e_i$ by $L_j$ multiplies its sole nonzero entry by $q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}$; conjugating $F_i:e_i\mapsto e_{i+1}$ gives the inverse exponent. Also $K_i$ has eigenvalue $q$ on $e_i$, $q^{-1}$ on $e_{i+1}$ and $1$ on every other basis vector, so $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $1,-1,0$ in those positions. Directly, $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $[E_i,F_i]$ is that diagonal matrix. Products $E_iE_j$ and $E_jE_i$ (and the corresponding $F$ products) both vanish when $|i-j|>1$; $E_i^2=F_i^2=0$, and each middle three-letter Serre product also vanishes because its matrix-unit indices do not compose. Thus every defining relation holds, and the quotient universal property [F1] gives the vector representation. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Define $\Delta$ on the free generators by the displayed formulas in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]]. The $\Delta(L_j)$ are mutually commuting units with the displayed inverses. Conjugation by $\Delta(L_j)$ gives the required weights on each of the two terms of $\Delta(E_i)$ and $\Delta(F_i)$, since each $K_i$ is a Laurent monomial in the commuting $L$'s. For any $i,j$, expansion gives $[\Delta(E_i),\Delta(F_j)]=[E_i,F_j]\otimes K_i+K_j^{-1}\otimes[E_i,F_j]+[E_i\otimes K_i,K_j^{-1}\otimes F_j]$. The last cross term is zero: its first product can be reordered as $q^{a_{ji}-a_{ij}}K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i=K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i$, which is its reverse product by [F3]. If $i\ne j$, the remaining terms vanish; if $i=j$, they sum to $\bigl(K_i\otimes K_i-K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\bigr)/(q-q^{-1})=\Delta\bigl((K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})\bigr)$. For $|i-j|>1$, $a_{ij}=0$ and the $K_i$ commute with $E_j,F_j$; expanding the two commutators therefore proves that the distant $E$ and $F$ relations are preserved. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\gamma=q+q^{-1}$ and $S_{ij}(X,Y)=X^2Y-\gamma XYX+YX^2$ for adjacent $i,j$. For the $E$ relation write $\Delta(E_s)=A_s+B_s$ with $A_s=E_s\otimes K_s$, $B_s=1\otimes E_s$. In each of the three words $iij,iji,jii$, choose an $A$ at each selected position and a $B$ at each other position, then move the selected $K$ factors to the right using $K_rE_s=q^{a_{rs}}E_sK_r$. Grouping the resulting 24 terms by the number of selected positions gives: degree $0$ in the first factor is $1\otimes S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)$; degree $3$ is $S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)\otimes K_i^2K_j$; degree $1$ has respective coefficients $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $1+q^{-2}-\gamma q^{-1}$ on $E_i\otimes E_iE_jK_i$, $E_i\otimes E_jE_iK_i$, $E_j\otimes E_i^2K_j$; degree $2$ has respective coefficients $q^{-2}+1-\gamma q^{-1}$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$ on $E_i^2\otimes E_jK_i^2$, $E_iE_j\otimes E_iK_iK_j$, $E_jE_i\otimes E_iK_jK_i$. All six mixed coefficients are zero by the definition of $\gamma$, and the two pure terms vanish by the defining Serre relation. Thus $\Delta$ preserves every positive Serre relation. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The assignment $\phi(L_j)=L_j^{-1}$, $\phi(E_i)=F_i$, $\phi(F_i)=E_i$ preserves the presentation: it exchanges the two weight relations, sends the mixed commutator to its negative with $K_i$ replaced by $K_i^{-1}$, and exchanges the distant and Serre relations. It is an involution. On generators $\Delta(F_i)=\tau(\phi\otimes\phi)\Delta(E_i)$, where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is an algebra isomorphism. Since step 1.3 proves that the positive Serre polynomial maps to zero, applying the algebra maps $\tau$ and $\phi\otimes\phi$ proves that the negative Serre polynomial maps to zero as well. Together steps 1.2–2.1 show every relation is killed, so [F1] descends $\Delta$ to the quotient. The counit assignment kills the relations directly: each relation becomes either $1=1$ or $0=0$, so it too descends. [given, F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Both counit composites and both iterated coproduct composites are algebra homomorphisms, so it suffices by [F2] to check generators. The maps $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$ return $L_j,E_i,F_i$ from their displayed formulas. On $L_j$, both iterated coproducts give $L_j\otimes L_j\otimes L_j$; on $E_i$, both give $E_i\otimes K_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes1\otimes E_i$; on $F_i$, both give $F_i\otimes1\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$. Hence $\Delta$ is coassociative with counit $\epsilon$. The vector representation of step 1.1 and the iterated coproduct therefore define actions on every $V_N^{\otimes n}$. They are finite sums and products of matrices with entries $0,1,q^{\pm1}$, so all entries lie in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

derivations.claim: Integral matrices. Write the iterated coproduct $E_i$ as its sum of single-position raising operators. The summand at position $j$ has coefficient $v^{h_i(w_{>j})}$; the lowering summand has coefficient $v^{-h_i(w_{<j})}$. A position cannot be used twice. For $a$ distinct raising positions, swapping two consecutive choices changes the exponent by $2$, since changing $i+1$ to $i$ increases $h_i$ by $2$. Summing the orders gives $v^{a(a-1)/2}[a]_v!$ times the coefficient using the original suffix counts: explicitly $\sum_{\pi\in S_a}v^{2\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}=v^{a(a-1)/2}[a]_v!$, as follows by inserting the largest letter, which multiplies the sum by $1+v^2+\cdots+v^{2(a-1)}$. The lowering calculation uses prefixes and the same identity. Therefore, over the generic field and then as integral matrices, $E_i^{(a)}e_w=\sum_{\substack{J\subseteq\{j:w_j=i+1\}\\|J|=a}}v^{a(a-1)/2+\sum_{j\in J}h_i(w_{>j})}e_{w(J\mapsto i)},\quad F_i^{(a)}e_w=\sum_{\substack{J\subseteq\{j:w_j=i\}\\|J|=a}}v^{a(a-1)/2-\sum_{j\in J}h_i(w_{<j})}e_{w(J\mapsto i+1)}.$ The toral generator acts on content $\alpha$ by $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_j\\t\end{smallmatrix}\right]_v$, integral by [F3]. Thus every generating matrix preserves $T$. No factorial is inverted after specialization.

Transport of the Hecke action. For $w_\mu=1^{\mu_1}\cdots N^{\mu_N}$ define $\theta_\mu(m_\mu T_d)=v^{\ell(d)}e_{w_\mu d}$. Every word of content $\mu$ occurs once, $\ell(d)=\operatorname{inv}(w_\mu d)$, and each coefficient is a unit; hence $\theta_\mu$ is an integral bijection. Standard Hecke multiplication on distinguished cosets gives an ascending swap with coefficient $1$, a descending swap with coefficient $q$ plus $(q-1)$ times the original coset, and coefficient $q$ when the two letters coincide. Multiplying the basis vectors by $v^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}$ changes the two unequal-letter swap coefficients to $v$, giving exactly the displayed tensor formula. Consequently this is an actual Hecke action, with quadratic and braid relations inherited from $H$, and $\theta=\bigoplus_\mu\theta_\mu$ is a right-module isomorphism.

Commutation can be checked locally. Put $j=i+1$. On the four two-letter words $ii,ij,ji,jj$, the nonzero local raising values are $E(ij)=ii$, $E(ji)=vii$, $E(jj)=v^{-1}ij+ji$, and the nonzero lowering values are $F(ii)=v^{-1}ij+ji$, $F(ij)=jj$, $F(ji)=vjj$. The Hecke values are $H(ii)=qii$, $H(ij)=vji$, $H(ji)=vij+(q-1)ji$, $H(jj)=qjj$. Substitution proves $EH=HE$, $FH=HF$: on $ij$ and $ji$ the raising composites give respectively $qii$ and $vqii$, and on $jj$ they give $vij+qji$; lowering gives the transposed three checks. With one active letter and one outside $\{i,j\}$ the suffix or inverse-prefix multiplier is $1$, and the outside letter has the same comparison with $i$ and $j$, so swapping or retaining that letter commutes with its replacement. With no active letter both operators are zero. Terms of the full coproduct acting outside the adjacent pair only see its total $h_i$, unchanged by its Hecke action; diagonal toral operators depend only on content. This proves commutation for $E_i,F_i,K_j$. Over the generic field divided powers commute too; since their integral matrices are given in step 1.1, their commutator entries are zero Laurent polynomials. Toral binomials commute by content. Thus $\rho$ has image in the actual integral commutant.

Orbit coordinates for that commutant. Fix source content $
u$ and split its sorted word into contiguous column blocks of lengths $
u_j$. For an $N	imes N$ nonnegative integer matrix $D=(d_{ij})$ of total $r$, with column sums $
u$ and row sums $\mu$, let $\mathcal W_D$ be the words containing exactly $d_{ij}$ letters $i$ in block $j$, and put $z_D=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W_D}v^{\operatorname{inv}_
u(w)}e_w,$ where $\operatorname{inv}_
u$ counts inversions separately inside those blocks. Within a block, pairing an ascending word and its descending swap in $yT_s=qy$ forces the descending coefficient to be $v$ times the ascending coefficient, since $v$ is a unit. Adjacent swaps connect every arrangement to the uniquely blockwise sorted word $w_D$. Hence all simultaneous $q$-eigenvectors for the source row subgroup are exactly the free span of the $z_D$, whose supports are disjoint and whose coefficient at $w_D$ is one. By the cyclic presentation [F2], evaluation at $e_{w_
u}$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_H(T_
u,T_\mu)$ with this eigenspace. Write $\xi_D$ for the map with that evaluation. These maps give an explicit integral basis, independently of any generic rank comparison, over every ring with a chosen invertible $v$.

The toral element $P_\mu=\prod_j\left[\begin{smallmatrix}K_j;0\\\mu_j\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ acts on content $\alpha$ by $\prod_j\left[\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_j\\\mu_j\end{smallmatrix}\right]_v$. If $\alpha\ne\mu$ and both sum to $r$, at least one $\alpha_j<\mu_j$, making that factor identically zero; if $\alpha=\mu$, every factor is one. Thus $\rho(P_\mu)=1_\mu$. For a diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(\mu)$ the orbit map $\xi_D$ is this projection. These conclusions remain identities at parameters where several $K_j$ eigenvalues coincide.

Define the triangular order, within fixed row and column sums, by all northeast and southwest rectangle sums $\sigma_{ab}(D)=\begin{cases}\sum_{s\le a,\ t\ge b}d_{st}&a<b,\\\sum_{s\ge a,\ t\le b}d_{st}&a>b.\end{cases}$ Write $D'\preceq D$ if every such sum is at most the corresponding sum for $D$. This is an actual partial order: differences of northeast rectangle sums recover each strictly upper entry, differences of southwest sums recover each strictly lower entry, and the fixed row sums then recover the diagonal. Put $\delta(D)=\sum_{i,j}|i-j|d_{ij}$ and $s(D)=\sum_{a\ne b}\sigma_{ab}(D)$. The diagonal-boundary sums give $\delta(D)=\sum_{a=1}^{N-1}(\sigma_{a,a+1}(D)+\sigma_{a+1,a}(D))$. Therefore $D'\prec D$ implies $\delta(D')\le\delta(D)$ and $s(D')<s(D)$. The pair $(\delta,s)$ of nonnegative integers supplies a terminating induction even when intermediate matrices have different row sums.

Extreme-column multiplication. Acting by $E_i^{(b)}$ on $z_D$ transfers $b$ letters from row $i+1$ to row $i$, distributed as $t_j$ among the column blocks, with $0\le t_j\le d_{i+1,j}$ and $\sum_jt_j=b$. Its expansion in step 4.1 has only the matrices $D+\sum_jt_j(E_{ij}-E_{i+1,j})$. Choosing the rightmost available columns greedily maximizes every suffix $\sum_{j\ge k}t_j$ and minimizes every prefix $\sum_{j\le k}t_j$. A transfer across the row boundary $i$ changes a northeast rectangle only when its row cutoff is $i$, by such a suffix; it changes a southwest rectangle only when its lower row cutoff is $i+1$, by the negative of such a prefix. Thus this greedy matrix dominates every other supported matrix in $\preceq$. For several $E_i$ executed in increasing $i$, the source row $i+1$ has not yet been changed, and each operation changes rectangle coordinates at its own boundary only. Consequently simultaneous greedy choices still give a single maximal supported matrix. If at each boundary the target row originally contains zero letters in every selected column, its coefficient is a Laurent unit: to obtain the blockwise sorted final word, all newly present $i$'s in those columns must have been raised, giving exactly one predecessor word and one subset. That predecessor is blockwise sorted, with coefficient one in $z_D$, and step 1.1 gives a single Laurent monomial. Earlier operations only depleted this target row, so its zero entries persist. Multiplying these monomials gives the claimed unit pivot, and uniqueness of successive row transfers rules out an additional path to the same final matrix.

The lower version is equally explicit. Acting by $F_i^{(b)}$ transfers letters from row $i$ to row $i+1$. Greedy selection of the leftmost available columns maximizes southwest prefix increments and minimizes northeast suffix decrements, hence gives the maximal matrix. Execute several $F_i$ in decreasing $i$; each source row is then unchanged before its turn, and the rectangle boundaries are again distinct. If all selected target entries are initially zero, the blockwise sorted final word has exactly one predecessor and chosen subset, so its coefficient is a Laurent monomial by the lowering formula of step 1.1. This proves the same maximal-support and unit-pivot assertion without invoking a Gaussian coefficient or cancelling one.

Upper elimination. Suppose $D$ has a strictly upper entry and let $k>0$ be the largest distance $j-i$ of such an entry. Set $b_i=d_{i,i+k}$ (zero when $i+k>N$) and $D_0=D-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i,i+k}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i+1,i+k},\qquad X=E_{N-1}^{(b_{N-1})}\cdots E_1^{(b_1)}.$ Zero terms with column index greater than $N$ are omitted. Thus $X$ executes its operations in increasing $i$. The rightmost nonzero column of source row $i+1$ in $D_0$ is at most $i+k$: its original distance-$k$ entry was removed, and the shifted entry from row $i$ is at $i+k$. There are at least $b_i$ letters at that column. Hence the greedy transfer selects exactly $b_i$ letters there and recovers $D$. Target row $i$ in $D_0$ has zero at column $i+k$, since that entire outer entry was removed and its added entry is at $i+k-1$. Step 7.1 therefore gives $X\xi_{D_0}=u_D\xi_D+\sum_{D'\prec D}a_{D'}\xi_{D'},\qquad u_D\in A^\times,\ a_{D'}\in A.$ Its source is still $\nu$, and its target row sum is the row sum of $D$, so these lower terms belong to that same Hom block. Also $\delta(D_0)=\delta(D)-\sum_i b_i<\delta(D)$. Every coefficient is explicitly obtained by the finite subset sums in step 1.1 and reading the blockwise sorted word coefficient of step 4.1.

Lower elimination. If $D$ is lower triangular but not diagonal, let $k>0$ be its largest lower distance and put $b_i=d_{i+1,i+1-k}$. Set $D_0=D-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i+1,i+1-k}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i,i+1-k},\qquad X=F_1^{(b_1)}\cdots F_{N-1}^{(b_{N-1})},$ with zero terms omitted when the column index is out of range. Now operations execute in decreasing $i$. The leftmost source column in row $i$ of $D_0$ is at least $i+1-k$, with at least $b_i$ letters there; the target entry at that column is zero. Therefore step 8.1 gives the same expansion with unique unit pivot at $D$, and again $\delta(D_0)=\delta(D)-\sum_i b_i$.

Exact recursive preimages and surjectivity. Induct on $(\delta(D),s(D))$. For a diagonal matrix use $R_D=P_\mu$ of step 5.1. In either non-diagonal case, $D_0$ has smaller first coordinate, while each $D'\prec D$ in steps 9.1–10.1 has a strictly smaller pair by step 6.1. With their already constructed preimages define $R_D=u_D^{-1}\left(XR_{D_0}-\sum_{D'\prec D}a_{D'}R_{D'}\right).$ This is a finite $A$-linear combination of ordered words in simple divided powers and toral weight projections, with completely specified coefficient extraction; $u_D^{-1}$ is only a Laurent monomial. Its image is exactly $\xi_D$. The finite matrix inventory and the decreasing nonnegative pair guarantee termination. Since the $\xi_D$ are the actual integral Hom basis, their preimages prove surjectivity. Tensoring this expression with any $A$-algebra gives the same basis and preimages; step 4.1 proves that the specialized commutant itself has this basis. Thus specialization commutes with the endomorphism construction, including nonflat specialization and roots of unity.

Identify the adjoint involution. In the coset basis equip $M^\mu$ with diagonal form $\langle m_\mu T_d,m_\mu T_eangle=\delta_{de}q^{\ell(d)}$. Under $	heta_\mu$ this becomes ordinary tensor dot product. To see that the involution of [F2] is its adjoint, work temporarily over $\mathbb Q(v)$ with the standard Hecke trace $t(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$, for which $t(T_x^*T_y)=\delta_{xy}q^{\ell(x)}$ by standard-basis multiplication. Write $p_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}q^{\ell(w)}$, so $m_\mu^2=p_\mu m_\mu$; the coset form is $t(x^*y)/p_\mu$ on $M^\mu$. If $f(m_
u)=y\in M^\mu\cap Hm_
u$, then $f^*(m_\mu)=y^*$ by the actual definition. For $x=m_
u h$ and $z=m_\mu k$, both adjoint pairings are $t(k^*yh)$: use $m_\mu y=p_\mu y$ in the first, $ym_
u=p_
u y$ in the second, and the trace property. Thus $*$ is the dot adjoint. The conclusion concerns equality of integral matrices, so it holds over $A$ and every specialization; the temporary nonzero $p_\mu$ is never divided in those rings.

The assignment $\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_j)=K_j$ reverses and preserves the generic defining relations: reversing the toral relation replaces its root exponent by the negative one; the mixed commutator and its right side are both fixed; the Serre polynomial is carried to the reversed negative polynomial. It fixes the toral binomials and exchanges divided powers, hence preserves $U_A$. Let $\beta=\mu+a(\epsilon_i-\epsilon_{i+1})$. For a chosen raising subset, subtracting the reverse lowering exponent in step 1.1 gives $a(\mu_i-\mu_{i+1})+a^2$, whereas $c_\beta/c_\mu=v^{-a(\mu_i-\mu_{i+1})-a^2}$. Thus the weighted dot form $\langle x,y\rangle_C=\langle x,Cy\rangle$ makes the raising and lowering matrices adjoint; all toral matrices are diagonal and self-adjoint. Its adjoint operator is $C^{-1}s^*C$. Equality on all integral generators, followed by reversal of products and linearity, proves $\rho(\tau(u))=C^{-1}\rho(u)^*C$ for every $u$.

Square-root-free matrices. In step 2.1 the permutation-module word basis is $b_w=v^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}e_w$. If raising a subset $J$ of $a$ positions changes $w$ to $w'$, counting inversions involving a changed letter gives $\operatorname{inv}(w)-\operatorname{inv}(w')=\sum_{j\in J}\bigl(\#i(w_{>j})-\#(i+1)(w_{<j})\bigr)+\binom a2.$ The final correction counts pairs of changed positions, counted incorrectly by changing each letter in isolation. Add the exponent in step 1.1 and use $\#(i+1)(w_{<j})+\#(i+1)(w_{>j})=\mu_{i+1}-1$. The coefficient in the $b$ basis is $v^{a(a-\mu_{i+1})+2\sum_{j\in J}\#i(w_{>j})}$. Scaling by $v^{a(\mu_{i+1}-a)}$ gives the displayed $q$-coefficient. For lowering, the analogous inversion difference is $\sum_{j\in J}(\#(i+1)(w_{<j})-\#i(w_{>j}))+\binom a2$, giving coefficient $v^{a(a-\mu_i)+2\sum_{j\in J}\#(i+1)(w_{<j})}$ and the asserted normalization. These define matrices over $B$. Their Hecke commutation follows from step 3.1 after the injective substitution $B\hookrightarrow A$, so all their polynomial commutator entries are zero already over $B$.

Over $B$ the permutation-basis Hecke formulas force equal coefficients for ascending and descending arrangements within each source block: an ascending word goes to its swap, a descending word to $q$ times its swap plus $(q-1)$ times itself, and the equation $yT_s=qy$ uses only the unit $q$. Thus the unweighted sums $\sum_{w\in\mathcal W_D}b_w$ give the same orbit Hom basis, denoted $\Phi_D$. The cross-block inversion count $d(D)=\sum_{j<k,\ a>b}d_{aj}d_{bk}$ is constant on $\mathcal W_D$, so $\Phi_D=v^{d(D)}\xi_D$ under extension to $A$. Repeat steps 6.1–11.1 directly with the normalized operators of step 14.1. Their supports and greedy maximal matrices are identical, and every unique pivot is now a single power of $q$, because every contributing subset coefficient is a power of $q$. The recursion therefore uses only $B$-coefficients and $q$-unit pivots and proves generation over $B$. The same orbit presentation and recursion work after every map $B\to R$. Finally, adjoining $z$ with $z^2=q$ gives $R'=R[z]/(z^2-q)$, free of rank two over $R$, with $z^{-1}=q^{-1}z$; it is faithfully flat even in characteristic two. Quantum assertions requiring a square root may be used there, while any specified map, equality, kernel, cokernel, or exact sequence already defined over $R$ descends by faithful flatness. The square-root-free generation proved here itself needs no such extension. At $r=0$ every construction is the identity map of $A$ or $B$, and at $N=1$ all matrices are diagonal, so the base case covers both edge cases. No Choice principle, generic rank argument, or nonunit denominator is used for generation.

Put $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$, $q=v^2$, $N\ge1$, $r\ge0$, $V=A^N$, and $T=V^{\otimes r}$. Let $U_{\mathbb Q(v)}(\mathfrak{gl}_N)$ have the presentation of [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]] with its indeterminate renamed $v$ and its diagonal generators written $K_j$. Define $U_A$ to be its $A$-subalgebra generated by $K_j^{\pm1}$, $E_i^{(a)}=E_i^a/[a]_v!$, $F_i^{(a)}=F_i^a/[a]_v!$, and
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_j;0\\t\end{bmatrix}=\prod_{s=1}^t\frac{K_jv^{1-s}-K_j^{-1}v^{s-1}}{v^s-v^{-s}}\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Use $K_je_b=v^{\delta_{jb}}e_b$, $E_ie_b=\delta_{b,i+1}e_i$, $F_ie_b=\delta_{b,i}e_{i+1}$ and the coproduct
$$\Delta(E_i)=1\otimes E_i+E_i\otimes K_iK_{i+1}^{-1},\qquad\Delta(F_i)=K_i^{-1}K_{i+1}\otimes F_i+F_i\otimes1,\qquad\Delta(K_j)=K_j\otimes K_j.$$
The resulting action preserves $T$ and commutes with the right $H_{A,q}(S_r)$ action
$$e_{\ldots ab\ldots}T_s=\begin{cases}v e_{\ldots ba\ldots}&a<b,\\q e_{\ldots aa\ldots}&a=b,\\(q-1)e_{\ldots ab\ldots}+v e_{\ldots ba\ldots}&a>b.\end{cases}$$
It gives a surjection
$$\rho:U_A\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{H_{A,q}(S_r)}(T)\cong S_A(N,r)$$
onto the actual permutation-module endomorphism algebra of [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]. Its composition-weight projections are
$$1_\mu=\rho\left(\prod_{j=1}^N\begin{bmatrix}K_j;0\\\mu_j\end{bmatrix}\right)\qquad(\mu\in\Lambda(N,r)).$$
Every statement survives any homomorphism $A\to R$ to a commutative ring, including parameters at arbitrary roots of unity; $S_A\otimes_A R$ is the actual specialized endomorphism algebra. The proof supplies a terminating exact divided-power expression for each integral orbit-basis map, with Laurent-unit pivots.

Let $\tau$ be the antiautomorphism $E_i\leftrightarrow F_i$, $K_j\mapsto K_j$, let $*$ be the current cellular antiautomorphism of $S_A$, and put $C=\sum_\mu c_\mu1_\mu$, $c_\mu=v^{-\sum_j\binom{\mu_j}{2}}$. Then
$$\rho(\tau(u))=C^{-1}\rho(u)^*C\qquad(u\in U_A).$$

There is also a square-root-free version over $B=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. On the permutation-module word basis define weight-block operators $\mathcal E_{i,a,\mu}$ and $\mathcal F_{i,a,\mu}$, zero outside content $\mu$, by replacing a subset $J$ of $a$ occurrences of $i+1$ by $i$, or of $i$ by $i+1$, respectively, with coefficients

Thus this generating assertion holds over every original coefficient ring with any unit $q$, whether or not $q$ has a square root. This assertion concerns the displayed polynomial action algebra; it does not assert a quantum group presentation over the original ring without choosing $v$.

For every dominant label weight $\lambda$, let $V_A=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda$ be the integral highest lattice inside the simple integrable module $L(\lambda)$, over $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. Then each label-weight component of $V_A$ is finite free of rank $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$, not merely torsionfree, and $V_A$ spans the field module. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V=\mathbb C^r$, $r\ge1$
([[def-schur-module-and-schur-polynomial-character]]), and let $\lambda$ be a
partition with $\ell(\lambda)\le r$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then
$$\operatorname{ch}S_\lambda(V)=\sum_T x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)},$$
the sum over all semistandard tableaux $T$ of shape $\lambda$ with entries in
$\{1,\dots,r\}$, where $\operatorname{wt}(T)=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ records the
multiplicity of each entry
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Moreover this polynomial
is the rank-$r$ Schur polynomial $s_\lambda(x_1,\dots,x_r)$ of
[[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]], i.e.
$$s_\lambda(x_1,\dots,x_r)=\frac{a_{\lambda+\delta_r}(x_1,\dots,x_r)}{a_{\delta_r}(x_1,\dots,x_r)}=\sum_Tx^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}$$
for $\ell(\lambda)\le r$, while $s_\lambda(x_1,\dots,x_r):=0$ and
$\operatorname{ch}S_\lambda(V)=0$ when $\ell(\lambda)>r$. In particular
$S_\lambda(V)\ne0$ if and only if $\ell(\lambda)\le r$, and the multiplicity of
the weight $\alpha$ in $S_\lambda(V)$ equals the number of semistandard
tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and weight $\alpha$; by
[[lem-bender-knuth-involutions-on-semistandard-tableaux]] this polynomial is
symmetric in $x_1,\dots,x_r$.

Fix $r\ge1$ and a skew shape $\nu/\lambda$ (for a partition shape take
$\lambda=\varnothing$), let $k\in\{1,\dots,r-1\}$, and let $T$ be a
semistandard skew tableau of shape $\nu/\lambda$ with entries in
$\{1,\dots,r\}$ ([[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]],
[[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). Call an entry $k$ or $k+1$ of
$T$ **free** if there is no $k+1$ respectively no $k$ in the same column. Then:

(i) the free positions in each row occupy consecutive cells of that row;
(ii) replacing in every row the free $k$'s and free $k+1$'s by their
complementary counts (if the row has $a_i$ free $k$'s and $b_i$ free $k+1$'s,
then after the replacement it has $b_i$ free $k$'s and $a_i$ free $k+1$'s in
the same free cells, the remaining entries unchanged, the free cells filled
from left to right by the $b_i$ copies of $k$ followed by the $a_i$ copies of
$k+1$) produces again a semistandard skew tableau $\sigma_k(T)$ of the same
shape, with entries in $\{1,\dots,r\}$;
(iii) $\sigma_k$ is an involution of the set of semistandard skew tableaux of
shape $\nu/\lambda$ with the same set of free positions, and
$\operatorname{wt}(\sigma_k(T))=s_k\operatorname{wt}(T)$, where $s_k$ is the
transposition of $k$ and $k+1$ acting on weights
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]], with weights read as vectors
in $\mathbb Z^r$).

Consequently, for every weight $\alpha\in\mathbb Z^r_{\ge0}$ the number of
semistandard skew tableaux of shape $\nu/\lambda$ and weight $\alpha$ equals
the number of weight $s_k\alpha$, and the generating function
$\sum_Tx^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}$, over semistandard skew tableaux of shape
$\nu/\lambda$ with entries in $\{1,\dots,r\}$, is symmetric in
$x_1,\dots,x_r$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Let $i\in I$ and let $T_{i,c,t}$ be the toral quantum binomials of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]
($i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$, $T_{i,c,0}=1$), inside the Drinfeld–Jimbo
algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]
with $U_A$ and its parts $U_A^-,U_A^0,U_A^+$ as in that definition. Write
$E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $E^{(a)}=E_i^{(a)}$, $F^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}$ for the divided
powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]] and put
$q=q_i$ inside the displayed formulas.

(i) **Divided-power multiplication.** For all $a,b\ge0$,
$$E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iE^{(a+b)},\qquad F^{(a)}F^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iF^{(a+b)}.$$

(ii) **Toral recursion and commutation.** For $t\ge1$,
$$T_{i,c,t}=\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-t+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+t-1}}{q_i^{\,t}-q_i^{\,-t}}\,T_{i,c,t-1}.$$
Each $T_{i,c,t}$ is a Laurent polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in
$\mathbb Q(q)$; the toral elements commute with one another and with all $K_h$.
For all $i,j$ and all $m\in\mathbb Z$ one has
$K_i^{\,m}T_{j,c,t}=T_{j,c,t}K_i^{\,m}$ if $i\ne j$, while
$E_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-2,t}E_i$, $E_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-a_{ij},t}E_j$,
$F_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+2,t}F_i$, $F_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+a_{ij},t}F_j$ for all $j$.
In particular $E_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0E_i$, $F_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0F_i$,
$T_{i,c,t}E_i=E_iT_{i,c+2,t}\in E_iU_A^0$ and
$T_{i,c,t}F_i=F_iT_{i,c-2,t}\in F_iU_A^0$: the toral factor can be moved to the
middle at the cost of a shift of the binomial index.

(iii) **Reordering identity.** For all $a,b\ge0$,

derivations.claim: Tableau support. In any semistandard tableau, each column has at most $k$ entries in $\{1,\ldots,k\}$; summing over columns gives $\sum_{j\le k}\mu_j\le\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j$. By [F4] the same inequality holds after permuting the content. Thus no weight $\lambda+a\alpha_i$, $a>0$, occurs. No weight $\lambda-a\alpha_i$ occurs when $a>m_i$: swapping its $i$th and $(i+1)$st coordinates makes its first $i$ coordinates sum to $\sum_{j\le i}\lambda_j+a-m_i$, violating that inequality. Negative coordinates also cannot occur. The type-$\lambda$ tableau is uniquely $T^\lambda$: the first content inequality is an equality forcing all $1$'s into row one, and successively equality for $k$ forces all $k$'s into row $k$. Hence the top weight line is $Ah$.

The highest map. The action in the Statement is a left action since $\tau$ reverses products. It has the stated weight labels by [F1]. Step 1.1 kills every $E_i^{(a)}h$ for $a>0$ and every $F_i^{(a)}h$ for $a>m_i$; the toral characters are those of weight $\lambda$. Thus [F3] gives a highest-module map $f:Q_A(\lambda)\to W_A^\lambda$. By the cell product and $B_{\rm cell}(h,h)=1$, $h\varphi_{T^\lambda T}=w_T$. Surjectivity in [F1] supplies an integral preimage under $\rho\tau$ of each of these endomorphisms, so $h$ generates the whole cell and $f$ is onto.

Cellular highest induction over any $R$. Put $I^{>\lambda}$ equal to the span of cellular shapes strictly dominating $\lambda$. This ideal is generated by the $1_\eta$ for $\eta>\lambda$: choose a finite order with larger shapes first, and use $\varphi_{S,T^\eta}1_\eta\varphi_{T^\eta,T}\equiv\varphi_{ST}$ modulo higher shapes, whose coefficient is $1$ by [F2]. Induction absorbs those higher terms in the already generated ideal; conversely each $1_\eta$ lies in $I^{>\lambda}$. The quotient $S_R1_\lambda/I^{>\lambda}1_\lambda$ has exactly the basis $\varphi_{T,T^\lambda}$ of shape $\lambda$: any semistandard type $\lambda$ in shape $\eta$ forces $\eta\unrhd\lambda$ by the column count in step 1.1, and shape $\lambda$ has the single second tableau $T^\lambda$. Star identifies this left cell with the right cell acted on by $s^*$; the weight-unit map sending its weight-$\mu$ basis vector to $(c_\mu/c_\lambda)w_T$ instead identifies it with the action $s\cdot w=wC^{-1}s^*C$ of the Statement. Its highest vector maps to $h$.

Integral isomorphism. In type $A_{N-1}$ the finite Weyl alternating quotient of [F3], on composition labels of fixed total $r$, is $\det(x_i^{\lambda_j+N-j})/\det(x_i^{N-j})$: the Weyl group permutes the $N$ coordinates, and multiplying numerator and denominator by the common monomial removes the half-sum shifts. This is the bialternant of [F4]. Consequently, for each weight $\mu$, [F3] and [F4] make the source and target finite free of the same rank $K_{\lambda\mu}$. The map in step 2.1 is graded, hence onto on each weight. Choose finite free bases and write its square matrix $D$; lifting the finitely many target basis vectors gives a matrix $P$ with $DP=I$. Therefore $\det(D)\det(P)=1$, and the adjugate formula gives an inverse matrix over $A$. Zero-rank weights have the unique empty inverse. Only finitely many weights occur, so these inverses assemble to $f^{-1}$. This proves the entire quotient presentation and the basis $b_T$. Concretely a preimage under the surjection of $\varphi_{T^\lambda T}$, followed by integral triangular spanning and highest-character evaluation, gives a representative of $b_T$ in $U_A^-$; different preimages give the same quotient class. No generic-rank argument replaces the proved integral surjection.

Let $X$ be the cyclic polynomial highest module in the Statement. By [F5], $X=U_R^-x$, so its composition weights lie in $\lambda-Q_+$, where $Q_+$ is the nonnegative simple-root cone. In particular $1_\eta X=0$ for every partition $\eta>\lambda$; such a partition is not in $\lambda-Q_+$. Step 2.2 then gives $I^{>\lambda}X=0$. The map $S_R1_\lambda\to X$, $s1_\lambda\mapsto sx$, is onto and factors through the left cell in step 2.2. It therefore gives the asserted quotient of $Q_R(\lambda)$. Apply this argument also to $Y=S_R\otimes_{S_R^+}R_\lambda$: its canonical generator has the stated toral character, is killed by all positive divided powers, and is fixed by $1_\lambda$. The last assertion follows because the integral toral projection $\prod_j\left[\begin{smallmatrix}K_j;0\\\lambda_j\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ is $1_\lambda$ and has highest-character value $1$. Thus $Y$ is a quotient of the left cell. Conversely the highest vector of that cell defines a surjection $Y$ onto it. Both compositions fix the cyclic highest generators, hence are identities, proving the induction equivalence. This is a direct cellular proof of the universal property.

Construct the form on the actual cell first. Give weight $\mu$ the scalar $d_\mu=c_\lambda/c_\mu$ times $B_{m cell}$ and pair distinct weights by zero. For $s=ho(u)$, [F1] gives $ho(	au(u))^*=CsC^{-1}$. On a homogeneous component, right multiplication by this conjugate contributes $c_

Put $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$, $q=v^2$, $N\ge1$, $r\ge0$, $V=A^N$, and $T=V^{\otimes r}$. Let $U_{\mathbb Q(v)}(\mathfrak{gl}_N)$ have the presentation of [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]] with its indeterminate renamed $v$ and its diagonal generators written $K_j$. Define $U_A$ to be its $A$-subalgebra generated by $K_j^{\pm1}$, $E_i^{(a)}=E_i^a/[a]_v!$, $F_i^{(a)}=F_i^a/[a]_v!$, and
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_j;0\\t\end{bmatrix}=\prod_{s=1}^t\frac{K_jv^{1-s}-K_j^{-1}v^{s-1}}{v^s-v^{-s}}\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Use $K_je_b=v^{\delta_{jb}}e_b$, $E_ie_b=\delta_{b,i+1}e_i$, $F_ie_b=\delta_{b,i}e_{i+1}$ and the coproduct
$$\Delta(E_i)=1\otimes E_i+E_i\otimes K_iK_{i+1}^{-1},\qquad\Delta(F_i)=K_i^{-1}K_{i+1}\otimes F_i+F_i\otimes1,\qquad\Delta(K_j)=K_j\otimes K_j.$$
The resulting action preserves $T$ and commutes with the right $H_{A,q}(S_r)$ action
$$e_{\ldots ab\ldots}T_s=\begin{cases}v e_{\ldots ba\ldots}&a<b,\\q e_{\ldots aa\ldots}&a=b,\\(q-1)e_{\ldots ab\ldots}+v e_{\ldots ba\ldots}&a>b.\end{cases}$$
It gives a surjection
$$\rho:U_A\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{H_{A,q}(S_r)}(T)\cong S_A(N,r)$$
onto the actual permutation-module endomorphism algebra of [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]. Its composition-weight projections are
$$1_\mu=\rho\left(\prod_{j=1}^N\begin{bmatrix}K_j;0\\\mu_j\end{bmatrix}\right)\qquad(\mu\in\Lambda(N,r)).$$
Every statement survives any homomorphism $A\to R$ to a commutative ring, including parameters at arbitrary roots of unity; $S_A\otimes_A R$ is the actual specialized endomorphism algebra. The proof supplies a terminating exact divided-power expression for each integral orbit-basis map, with Laurent-unit pivots.

$$\rho(\tau(u))=C^{-1}\rho(u)^*C\qquad(u\in U_A).$$

There is also a square-root-free version over $B=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. On the permutation-module word basis define weight-block operators $\mathcal E_{i,a,\mu}$ and $\mathcal F_{i,a,\mu}$, zero outside content $\mu$, by replacing a subset $J$ of $a$ occurrences of $i+1$ by $i$, or of $i$ by $i+1$, respectively, with coefficients

Over every commutative $A$-algebra $R$, every cyclic polynomial left $U_R$-module of degree $r$, generated by a vector of weight $\lambda$ killed by every positive divided generator, is a quotient of $Q_R(\lambda)$. Equivalently, the left Weyl cell is the polynomial highest-induced module $S_R\otimes_{S_R^+}R_\lambda$, where $S_R^+$ is the image of the integral toral-positive subalgebra and $R_\lambda$ is its highest character. This statement includes the zero module and uses the actual composition-weight projections, rather than separation of specialized $K_j$ eigenvalues.
